title: Hey folks - curious about the state of the industry.
author: theEsel01
selftext:
As a gamedev I am curious. How many people here have created games that are actually shipped to Steam (or similar) and are making real money. Are you able to finish and polish games aswell as actually shipping them.

Would love to hear your experiences.

Why do I ask... I personally have a feeling that ai gets you far... but to reach 100% of polish... thats a whole other story.

comments.author: EliasWick
comments.body:
People here definitely won't agree with me. However, as someone who have modded and created games for 20+ years, worked in AAA and used Unreal Engine for the past 10+ years, I believe I have a resonable take on it all.

Also a disclaimer: I don't like or want to use AI for game development. I make video games because it's fun, AI ruines that fun for me personally. But of course, we're all different.

You can use AI and ship a fully functional game on steam, it is absolutely possible. Is it going to be good? Definitely not.

You can use AI to write parts of your code, automate stuff, but you still need to be a good game developer to actually make something that works. A good design is not something AI will ever be able to serve you on a silver platter. Game development requires constant prototyping, redesigning, and most of all playtesting. Playtesting is not something AI can do and won't for a long time.

If you want to make a good game, you need to work hard, it will take years, and you will likely fail the first few times.

Since you mentioned money in your post, I unfortunately already know why you find it lucrative. Game development is not rainbows and sunshine, it's A LOT of work, and often for pennies.

Don't make a game if you want to rely on AI guiding you. If you use enough AI, it will be very expensive and your code base will be awful. AI can't design cohesively across all domains of game development.

replies.author: MorbilyABeast
replies.body:
"You can use Al and ship a fully functional game on steam, it is absolutely possible. Is it going to be good? Definitely not." 

Your bias is showing here. You even discredit yourself in the next sentence. It is not definitive at all. If you have an intuition fot something interesting fun and that works within game design then it will be siccessfull. The average consumer doesnt care what tool you used. The passion will show in the end product. 

With that being said people make slop, they try to one shot a "fun game". They failed before they even began particularly due to the fact that they offloaded all decisions to ai in regards to game design. And ai can only guess what works and what doesnt. Its vastly different to reality of humans actually playing the game and what their experience is.

Using it as a tool is completely viable. You make the decisions. If you make poor design decisions it will fail either way. People wont want to play it anyways. Many game devs that dont use ai have failed games. People didnt magically want to play their game because it didnt use ai and vice versa

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
I am 100% biased, and it's based on feelings, experiences, and facts.

The average consumer definitely considers what tools you used. "Recent industry data shows that games disclosing generative AI usage suffer a severe sales penalty, experiencing a 40% to 53% drop in user engagement and reviews compared to non-AI titles." - https://www.techpowerup.com/350230/games-made-with-gen-ai-suffer-up-to-53-worse-sales-on-steam

I also haven't defined what my view on successful games would be. For instance Wordle is a successful game, but my scope is higher and more refined for this question. Most games released today on Steam are not good in my opinion. I'm throwing out a number right now, but probably 0.5% of them all might be resonably good, if even that.

A good game is a game you will remember the rest of your life. I tell you... there aren't many of those... and again: "I" don't believe AI will be able to make that for a looooooong time.

replies.author: MorbilyABeast
replies.body: About the stats that is understandable in the current state. Most use cases are literally slop or companies that have the resources to hire people but dont. Both cases are unacceptable. I do think loud and vocal anti ai users will avoid them. And it may have an effect on sales even in the future as more games use ai as a tool. But I do think it will resolve to something less hysterical the kore projects come out with people using it for something interesting , and not offloading every game design decision to the robot bout from the heart and just using it to code the mechanics. This is what ia m doing for example.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
That's a good point. What AI should mean for people (in my opinion), is that: You can now create faster, make more and have a chance to make it better.

Most tools in Unreal Engine today requires highly professional experience to understand and use properly. For instance the motion matching system is complex if you want to use it properly. No AI will help with that, you have to learn and spend time to get good.

Code has been simplified a lot... but AI will leave ghost code or unusable / deprecated stuff unless you monitor it. I personally believe that 90% (just throwing out a number again), don't maintain their generated AI code. Most games generated by AI won't end up on Steam either.

replies.author: MorbilyABeast
replies.body:
Yes thats reasonable. And id even add onto that not just faster and better, but also just having the chance at all. The accessibility for people with ideas that can iterate and experiment will make for interesting games in the future. People who would have otherwise not been able to do so, myself included!

But yeah engines do require some due diligence. But since using claude to code my game i can honestly say it had unlocked the engine for me. Just by being so deep in the systems themselves to get what i want and troubleshooting different aspects of the engine. Its really helped me push through moments of doubt, or saved me countless hours of surfing google , asking in doscord to peoplle who patronise you , or an hour long youtube video for a niche answer.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
I am happy you have found what works for you! I think the toxicity of AI bros come in whenever you try to start pushing AI onto people.

I am a musician and play a lot of piano, but me going to some app and generating piano music isn't going to be the same. For me coding and debugging is fun, but it surely isn't for everyone.

Having access to advanced information super fast is lovely though. I am not sure about your background or where you are in your game dev journey. But people had 40+ google tabs open with stack overflow and other sites to sometimes figure out why something didn't work the way you wanted it to. Being able to ask AI when you can't figure something out is good. But personally I enjoy the challenge, I feel like it doesn't stagnate my brain and knowledge.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
AI hasn't been around long enough at a high enough level for any larger projects to be completed using it. Not at high quality standards anyway. That's why you have a lot of low polish slop out there. I would agree on your polish statement and push it even further. Youtube 'Sky is Falling' videos on AI making games claim to make minecraft or some other bullshit in one 24 hour session. In reality the game they showcase only has 1% of the cohesion and content that Minecraft has, missing everything that makes the game feel like a game (sound, visual cues, rewards, etc, as well as just not even encompassing all of the complex systems or the variety of things available). It doesn't factor in that you still have 99% of the game to go and every subsequent percent is harder than the last because you then have to bind it together with all existing content.

Most AI game devs get started and think, "Wow look at me go! This is so easy." And then a few weeks pass and they start running into issues where they can't get features right, and they're iterating 100 times for a single one, and honestly most probably lose their motivation on the first few stumbling blocks and drop their projects entirely because they deem them too hard.

If someone isn't prepared to learn and actually do work in this field, they're not going to release anything more than slop IMO.  But that learning and polishing is a process, and it takes time. We'll see more eventually, but again, we're still in the pioneering phases of all of this. It hasn't even been a year since AI hit that point of, "Wow this is actually happening."
